R_H1.passageTitle: A Jacket and an Umbrella in Melbourne

passages.label: A
passages.text: In Melbourne, the same street may be sunny in the morning and cloudy, windy and cold later. The Australian Bureau of Meteorology explains why the change can feel so sudden. Melbourne stands between two very different places. Australia's hot, dry centre is to the north, and the cold Southern Ocean is to the south.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Southern Victoria is also in a part of the world where strong winds often move from west to east. These winds carry weather systems across Melbourne quickly, and a day may begin sunny and become windy later, and a weather system called a cold front can cross the city fast. It brings cooler air from the ocean. Weather systems carried by these prevailing winds can bring quick changes to the temperature and the amount of rain in the same part of the city.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The Bureau describes a common sequence in which winds from the north bring clear skies and higher temperatures before the front reaches the city. When the cooler air arrives, the temperature falls and clouds move in, sometimes bringing rain or even a thunderstorm. A fast-moving front can make the change seem sudden because the conditions shift within minutes. After the sun comes out, a park may still look wet, and some streets can stay wet for a long time after a storm.

passages.label: D
passages.text: A warm morning can feel like spring, and a sudden rainy spell can then feel more like autumn or winter. The seasons on the calendar stay the same. What changes is the air over the city, and a jacket and an umbrella can both be useful during an afternoon with short periods of rainfall.

passages.label: E
passages.text: The climate over a whole year is more predictable. Official figures say January and February are usually the warmest months, while June and July are generally the coolest. October has the highest average monthly rainfall, and summer afternoons near Port Phillip Bay can feel cooler when a breeze comes in from the water. These patterns help people make plans, even though the weather on a particular day may take them by surprise.

R_H2.passageTitle: More Than One Season Map for Australia

passages.label: A
passages.text: What counts as a new season depends on where you are. In southern Australia, the Bureau of Meteorology calls December, January and February summer. June, July and August are winter. Spring and autumn are the three-month periods between them, and the scheme follows large changes in heat and daylight in cities including Melbourne.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Northern Australia often uses two seasons based on rainfall. The rainy season generally runs from October to April. The dry season generally runs from May to September. One cloudy afternoon can happen in either period. A long stretch of sunny or wet days tells more about the time of year than the sky on one day.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Australia also has Indigenous calendars. Indigenous people are Australia's first peoples. Their local communities have watched plants, animals and weather for thousands of years. Their calendars may have three, five or six seasons. One time of year may begin when a plant flowers or when an animal moves to a new place. These calendars show that local climate knowledge can describe one place better than one national list. The sun can feel hot on a beach and cooler in the mountains, and Australia also has inland desert weather.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Daylight also varies throughout the year. The sky can grow dark before dinner in winter. Southern Australia has longer daylight in summer and shorter days in winter. The longer days are usually warm, while the shorter days are usually cold. At the shortest day, Hobart has about nine hours of daylight, while Darwin has about eleven and a half. At the longest day, Hobart has about fifteen hours, but Darwin has about twelve and a half. The difference is smaller in the tropical north. There, the amount of rain tells people more about the time of year than the temperature does.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Southern days are often warm in summer and cold in winter. A single windy day can happen at any time. By looking at changes over weeks, people in Melbourne, tropical Darwin and different Indigenous communities can each describe the local climate in a way that helps them understand their part of Australia.

R_H3.passageTitle: Rain, Rice and Cuba's Two Seasons

passages.label: A
passages.text: Cuba has a tropical climate with two main periods in its annual weather pattern. The rainy season extends from May to October and is sometimes called summer, whereas the dry period, sometimes called winter, lasts from November to April. The word winter can suggest cold to an overseas visitor. The plains generally stay warm, while temperatures can be lower in the high mountains.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The amount of rain changes with location. The west generally receives more rainfall than the east. The sky can turn from sunny to cloudy as a thunderstorm develops. Hurricanes can affect Cuba from June to November, during summer and autumn in a four-season calendar. Brief periods of windy, wet weather can make a difference to people who work on farms. Fields near a river can stay green after drier ground turns brown.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Rice is grown mostly near Cuba's western coast. In an older country profile, the Food and Agriculture Organization describes two rice-growing seasons. In the spring or wet season, planting takes place from April to July. Harvesting follows from October to December. In the dry season, planting is from December to March and harvesting is from April to July.

passages.label: D
passages.text: These seasonal conditions influence how farmers sow. In the wet period, seed may be spread by aeroplane, whereas in the dry period a seed drill may be used. This machine places seed in the soil. The decision partly depends on the amount of water in the field, which helps explain why the two growing periods are associated with different methods.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Very heavy rain and strong winds can damage crops, and too little rain can also cause serious problems. A Food and Agriculture Organization report describes hurricanes, floods and long dry periods as hazards for agriculture in the Caribbean. Farmers may need to save water in a dry period and protect their fields before a storm. Cuba's two season names help organise the year, but farm decisions also depend on the water already in a particular field.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why might the word winter cause confusion for a visitor?
options: It means the rainy period occurs only in the western hills.
It tells the reader that Cuba uses no name for the warmer part of the year.
It names the dry part of the year, when much of the lowland is still warm.
It gives the same temperature for the mountains and plains.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Two farms are in the same part of the year. Why might they still have different water conditions?
options: Rainfall can differ across places and a field near a river may stay green longer than nearby drier land.
Fields at the same point on the calendar must have the same amount of water.
Only the name of the season matters once farmers know the planting date.
The field farther from every source of water always receives more rain.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How are a short storm and the island's hurricane period described differently?
options: Every short storm lasts until the hurricane period ends.
The hurricane period describes what happens during one afternoon only.
Cloudy conditions on a single day mean the island has reached November.
A thunderstorm can change the sky quickly, while hurricanes may affect the island during a range of months.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A farm plans to harvest the crop it planted in the wet season. Which plan matches both the stated calendar and a problem the farm may need to prepare for?
options: Harvest in spring and assume the fields cannot be affected by wind.
Harvest between October and December and prepare to protect the field if a strong storm approaches.
Begin harvesting in March because the old profile treats that month as the end of the wet harvest.
Plan only one harvest day, relying on the season name for its exact weather.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which order describes the dry-season rice cycle in the profile?
options: Plant between December and March and gather the crop from April to July.
Plant between April and July and gather the dry crop from October to December.
Plant in October and gather it before December starts.
Gather the crop between December and March and plant it again each April.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What does the article add to the older profile's dates to help explain choices at planting time?
options: It describes the same method for every field in the two cycles.
It shows that every farmer has to start planting on the same day.
It explains how differences in field water can lead to different ways of sowing.
It says the wet period always uses planting by machine under dry ground.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What is the role of a seed drill in the example?
options: It measures the strength of winds over Cuba.
It tells the pilot which hills receive more rain.
It stores harvested rice until the dry period.
It puts the seed into the ground.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why might a farmer plan both to keep water and to protect a field from a storm?
options: Strong wind helps crops so long as the season is wet.
Too little water creates one kind of risk and heavy rain or wind creates another.
Heavy rain and a dry spell always cause exactly the same damage.
Saving water makes it impossible for a storm to reach the field.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A farmer knows the broad season and is deciding how to sow rice. What else is needed before deciding?
options: The temperature suggested by the word winter is enough to choose a method.
The calendar for a different country would determine the best equipment.
Check how much water is actually in that field as well as knowing which season it is.
The amount of water in the field matters only after all the crop is cut.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which statement connects the passage's account of the climate and the farm work?
options: A single weather change makes the two rice cycles useless.
Once a season is named, everyone uses a single method on the island.
Rain affects the crop, but differences among fields have no effect on decisions.
The two parts of the year help organise planting and harvest, while work depends on what is happening in a field.
